stem: A 62-year-old male presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm. His 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Troponin I is elevated. What is the priority nursing action?

options.text: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and reassess pain in 5 minutes
options.why: Nitroglycerin does not reopen the occluded artery and must be used cautiously in inferior MI because of possible RV involvement and preload-dependent hypotension.

options.text: Notify the interventional cardiology team and prepare for emergent PCI
options.why: This patient is showing signs of STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF = inferior wall MI) with elevated troponin and classic chest pain. Time is myocardium; the gold standard is PCI within 90 minutes.

options.text: Start an IV and draw additional labs for CBC and electrolytes
options.why: IV access and labs are needed but are done in parallel and must not delay activation of the cath lab.

options.text: Monitor vital signs and place the patient on continuous ECG telemetry.
options.why: Monitoring is supportive only; it does not address the occluded coronary artery, which needs reperfusion.

takeaway: In STEMI, the priority is rapid reperfusion: activate the cath lab for PCI with a door-to-balloon goal of 90 minutes or less.

stem: A 74-year-old patient undergoes a carotid endarterectomy (CEA) for 80% stenosis of the right carotid artery. Postoperatively, the nurse notes a hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and right facial droop. What is the priority nursing action?

options.text: Suction the patient's airway to prevent aspiration
options.why: Suctioning may be needed if secretions pool, but it does not address the cause; the provider must be told of the new deficits.

options.text: Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees
options.why: Positioning can reduce aspiration risk but is a comfort/safety measure, not the priority response to new cranial nerve findings.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately due to possible cranial nerve injury
options.why: These signs suggest cranial nerve damage (CN IX, X, or XII), a possible complication of CEA. Immediate reporting is crucial to prevent aspiration, airway compromise, or delayed neurologic decline.
Aspirin does not treat nerve injury and giving anything by mouth with impaired swallowing risks aspiration.

takeaway: Hoarseness, dysphagia, or facial/tongue deviation after carotid endarterectomy suggests cranial nerve injury; report it promptly and protect the airway.

stem: A patient presents with chest pain, troponin elevation, and ST depression in leads V4–V6. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.why: STEMI requires ST elevation in contiguous leads, not ST depression.
ST depression with positive biomarkers = NSTEMI. STEMI shows ST elevation.
Stable angina is exertional, relieved by rest, and does not raise troponin.
Vasospastic angina typically causes transient ST elevation, usually without sustained troponin rise.

takeaway: Ischemic symptoms plus elevated troponin without ST elevation is an NSTEMI.

stem: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF suggests which MI location and artery?

options.why: Anterior MI shows ST elevation in V1–V4 and is caused by LAD occlusion.
Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) usually involves the RCA (sometimes the LCx).
Lateral MI shows changes in I, aVL, V5–V6.
Posterior MI shows ST depression in V1–V3; left main occlusion causes widespread changes, often with aVR elevation.

takeaway: Leads II, III, and aVF view the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery.

stem: A patient presents with sudden, severe leg pain, pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis. Which is the first nursing priority intervention?

options.why: Immediate IV heparin is standard to stop clot propagation, but the book keys emergent surgical evaluation as the first priority because paralysis signals a threatened limb.
An ABI delays definitive care and adds little when the limb is pulseless and paralyzed.
Acute arterial occlusion is a surgical emergency; motor loss means the limb is threatened and needs urgent revascularization.
Heat increases metabolic demand in ischemic tissue and can burn an insensate limb.

takeaway: Acute limb ischemia (the 6 Ps, especially paralysis) is a surgical emergency; anticoagulate and get emergent vascular surgery evaluation.
flag: Debatable key: AHA/ACC PAD guidelines call for immediate IV heparin (unless contraindicated) together with emergent vascular surgery evaluation, so A is also defensible as a first action.

stem: A patient post-carotid endarterectomy suddenly develops unilateral weakness and slurred speech. What should the nurse suspect?

options.why: Hyperperfusion syndrome usually presents days later with headache, seizures, or hypertension, not sudden focal deficits right after surgery.
Intracerebral hemorrhage is possible but less common than acute thrombosis at the endarterectomy site.
Immediate neuro change after endarterectomy = thrombosis or occlusion at the operative site.
Delirium causes fluctuating attention and cognition, not unilateral motor weakness.

takeaway: New focal neurologic deficits right after carotid endarterectomy suggest acute carotid thrombosis or embolism; notify the surgeon immediately.

stem: A patient reports tearing chest pain radiating to the back, with unequal BP in arms. What is the most likely condition?

options.why: Classic dissection = tearing pain radiating to the back plus asymmetric arm blood pressures.
MI pain is typically pressure-like and does not cause a significant arm-to-arm BP difference.
PE causes pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and hypoxemia rather than tearing back pain with BP asymmetry.
Pericarditis causes sharp pain relieved by sitting forward, with a friction rub.

takeaway: Tearing chest/back pain with unequal arm blood pressures is aortic dissection until proven otherwise.

stem: Following CABG, the nurse notes chest tube drainage of 350 mL in 1 hour. What is the priority?

options.why: Watching drainage of this volume delays treatment of likely surgical bleeding and risks tamponade or shock.
Volume may be needed, but it does not stop the bleeding; the surgeon must be notified.
Chest tube output over 200 mL/hr = surgical bleeding, an emergency that may need return to the OR.
Repositioning can help drain pooled blood but does not address active hemorrhage.

takeaway: Chest tube output over 200 mL/hr after cardiac surgery suggests surgical bleeding; notify the surgeon immediately.

stem: A patient with acute pulmonary edema presents with pink frothy sputum, tachypnea, and hypoxemia. First-line treatment?

options.why: There is no sign of infection; antibiotics do not relieve pulmonary congestion.
Fluids worsen volume overload and pulmonary edema.
Pulmonary edema = preload reduction (loop diuretics) plus oxygen support.
Epinephrine is for anaphylaxis or arrest and raises myocardial oxygen demand.

takeaway: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is treated with oxygen/ventilatory support and preload reduction (IV loop diuretics, nitrates).

stem: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD) indicates:

options.why: Tension pneumothorax causes hypotension and JVD but with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation, not muffled heart sounds.
Beck's triad = cardiac tamponade.
Cardiogenic shock causes hypotension and JVD but heart sounds are not muffled by fluid.
PE may cause hypotension and JVD but not muffled heart sounds.

takeaway: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) signals cardiac tamponade.

stem: A patient post-cardiac cath develops chest pain, hypotension, and ST elevation. Which complication is most likely?

options.why: Retroperitoneal bleeding causes hypotension and back/flank pain but not ST elevation.
Acute coronary dissection or thrombosis can occur post-cath and present as STEMI.
Vasovagal reactions cause hypotension and bradycardia without ST elevation.
Pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation with positional pain, usually not acute hypotension right after a cath.

takeaway: New chest pain with ST elevation after cardiac catheterization suggests acute coronary dissection or closure.

stem: Which hemodynamic profile is consistent with cardiogenic shock?

options.why: Cardiogenic shock = pump failure: high filling pressures (preload) with low CO/CI.
Low filling pressures with high output fit early distributive shock, not pump failure.
Low SVR with high CO is the pattern of septic (distributive) shock; cardiogenic shock has high SVR.
Pump failure raises filling pressures; normal pressures with low CO are not typical.

takeaway: Cardiogenic shock: high CVP and PAWP, low CO/CI, high SVR.

stem: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients are at high risk for:

options.why: Aortic rupture is linked to aneurysm or connective tissue disease, not HCM.

options.text: Sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmias
options.why: HCM predisposes to lethal ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, especially in young people and athletes.
Tamponade is not a typical complication of HCM.
HCM is not a primary risk factor for PE.

takeaway: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmias.

stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation has a rapid ventricular response and unstable BP. What is a priority intervention?

options.why: Beta-blockers can worsen hypotension in an unstable patient; they are for stable rate control.
Unstable AFib = immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Anticoagulation is important but does not correct instability; it should not delay cardioversion.
Adenosine does not convert atrial fibrillation and is not indicated.

takeaway: Any tachyarrhythmia with a pulse causing instability (hypotension, shock, altered mental status) needs synchronized cardioversion.

stem: A patient with acute decompensated HF presents with S3 gallop, dyspnea, and pulmonary rales. Which finding requires urgent intervention?

options.why: An elevated BNP confirms HF but is a lab value, not an immediately life-threatening finding.
A reduced EF describes chronic function and is not an acute emergency on its own.
Pink frothy sputum = acute pulmonary edema, an emergency needing immediate treatment.
Orthopnea is common in HF and expected; it is less urgent than frank pulmonary edema.

takeaway: Pink frothy sputum signals flash pulmonary edema and needs immediate oxygen and preload reduction.

stem: Which drug is first-line for a hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage?

options.why: Hypertensive emergency = IV titratable antihypertensives such as labetalol or nitroprusside.
Oral agents are too slow and not titratable for an emergency; clonidine is for urgency, not emergency.
Sublingual nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous BP drops and is no longer recommended.
Digoxin is not an antihypertensive.

takeaway: Hypertensive emergency needs IV titratable agents (labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroprusside) with controlled BP reduction.

stem: A patient develops acute pulmonary edema and a new loud systolic murmur after an MI. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.why: VSR also causes a new holosystolic murmur, but it usually presents with biventricular failure and a step-up in oxygen saturation; abrupt pulmonary edema points more to acute MR.
Pericarditis causes a friction rub, not a loud systolic murmur with pulmonary edema.

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture with severe MR
options.why: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation, leading to pulmonary edema and shock.
Dissection may cause a diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, not a new systolic murmur after MI.

takeaway: A new systolic murmur with sudden pulmonary edema 2–7 days after MI suggests papillary muscle rupture with acute severe mitral regurgitation.

stem: A patient presents with chest pain at rest, negative troponins, and transient ST depression. What is the diagnosis?

options.why: STEMI has ST elevation and positive biomarkers.
NSTEMI would have positive troponins.
Unstable angina = ischemia (rest pain, transient ST changes) without biomarker elevation.
Stable angina is predictable and exertional, not occurring at rest.

takeaway: Rest angina with ECG changes but normal troponin is unstable angina.

stem: A patient involved in a motor vehicle crash presents with hypotension, tachycardia, severe back pain, and rapidly expanding abdominal girth. Which finding is most concerning for aortic rupture?

options.why: Flank bruising suggests retroperitoneal bleeding but develops late and is not specific to the aorta.
Loss of distal pulses with shock strongly suggests aortic rupture/dissection compromising flow.
Epigastric pain is nonspecific and can come from many abdominal injuries.
Rupture causes hemorrhagic shock, not hypertension with bounding pulses.

takeaway: In trauma with shock and back pain, absent or diminished femoral pulses point to aortic injury.

stem: A patient undergoes transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Post-procedure, the nurse should closely monitor for:

options.why: Hyperkalemia is not a typical TAVR complication.
Coronary obstruction can occur but is rare compared with conduction problems.
The valve sits near the conduction system; TAVR often causes new LBBB or heart block, so pacing may be needed.
Tamponade from annular or ventricular perforation is possible but uncommon.

takeaway: After TAVR, monitor closely for new heart block or LBBB; a permanent pacemaker is a common need.

stem: A hypotensive patient with sudden dyspnea, syncope, and new RV dilation on bedside echo most likely has a massive PE. No bleeding risks are present. Best immediate therapy?

options.why: Anticoagulation alone does not rapidly relieve obstruction in massive (high-risk) PE with hypotension.
In massive PE with hypotension and no contraindications, systemic tPA improves perfusion and survival compared with anticoagulation alone.
Filters are for patients who cannot be anticoagulated; they do not treat the existing clot.
Catheter-based therapy is an option when lysis is contraindicated or fails, not the first-line choice here.

takeaway: Massive PE with hypotension and no bleeding contraindication: give systemic thrombolysis.

stem: A patient has a high clinical probability of PE. The CT scanner is unavailable for several hours, and there are no contraindications to anticoagulation. Next best step?

options.why: Delaying treatment in high-probability PE risks clot extension and death.
With high pretest probability and no bleeding risk, do not delay heparin until imaging.
D-dimer is useful only to rule out PE in low-probability patients; it does not change management here.
Aspirin is not adequate treatment for venous thromboembolism.

takeaway: With high clinical suspicion for PE and no contraindication, start anticoagulation before imaging confirms the diagnosis.

stem: Vent settings for moderate ARDS (P/F 110) should prioritize:

options.text: VT 8–10 mL/kg PBW; keep plateau <35 cmH₂O
options.why: These volumes and plateau limits are too high and increase ventilator-induced lung injury.

options.text: VT 6 mL/kg PBW; keep plateau <30 cmH₂O; apply appropriate PEEP
options.why: Low-tidal-volume ventilation (ARDSNet) reduces mortality; keep plateau 30 cmH₂O or less with adequate PEEP.

options.text: VT 10 mL/kg PBW; low PEEP strategy
options.why: High volumes with low PEEP cause volutrauma and atelectrauma.

options.text: VT 6 mL/kg PBW with zero PEEP
options.why: Zero PEEP allows alveolar collapse and worsens hypoxemia in ARDS.

takeaway: ARDS lung-protective ventilation: VT 4–8 (target 6) mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau 30 cmH₂O or less, adequate PEEP.

stem: In which patient is prone positioning most strongly indicated?

options.why: A P/F of 280 is mild hypoxemia; proning is not indicated.
This is moderate ARDS above the threshold where proning shows a mortality benefit.
Strong evidence supports early, prolonged prone positioning (often 12–16 h/day or more) in moderate–severe ARDS with P/F 150 or less on high FiO₂/PEEP.

options.text: P/F 220 with CXR showing lobar pneumonia
options.why: Unilateral lobar pneumonia with P/F 220 does not meet criteria for proning.

takeaway: Prone positioning is indicated in ARDS with P/F below 150 despite FiO₂ 0.6 or more and PEEP 5 or more.

stem: Witnessed aspiration of gastric contents during a seizure; now hypoxemic with wheeze and coughing. First priority?

options.why: Early aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury; antibiotics are given only if infection is suspected or develops.
Primary therapy for aspiration is airway clearance and protection plus oxygenation.
Corticosteroids have not been shown to improve outcomes in aspiration pneumonitis.
A PPI does not treat aspiration that has already occurred.

takeaway: After witnessed aspiration, clear the airway and support oxygenation first; routine antibiotics and steroids are not indicated.

stem: Which intervention has proven benefit in reducing ventilator-associated pneumonia?

options.why: Routine daily circuit changes do not reduce VAP; circuits are changed only when soiled or malfunctioning.
Head-of-bed elevation consistently reduces VAP risk by limiting aspiration.
Chest physiotherapy is not a proven VAP-prevention measure.
Fluid overload worsens lung function and does not prevent VAP.

takeaway: Keep the head of the bed at 30–45 degrees as part of the VAP prevention bundle.

stem: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 68, tachypnea; alert, using accessory muscles; no facial trauma. Best initial support?

options.why: Intubation is for patients who fail or cannot tolerate NIV, or who cannot protect the airway; this patient is alert.
For acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g., COPD exacerbation), NIV reduces intubation and mortality when there are no contraindications such as inability to protect the airway.
This is not a treatment; high-flow nasal cannula is not contraindicated, though BiPAP is preferred for hypercapnia.
CPAP alone gives no inspiratory pressure support and does little to clear CO₂.

takeaway: Alert patients with acute hypercapnic acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35) should get a BiPAP trial first.

stem: Patient in severe asthma attack is tiring; ABG changes from PaCO₂ 30 to 40 despite ongoing distress. Best next step?

options.why: A 'normal' PaCO₂ in a distressed asthmatic is not improvement; discharge would be dangerous.
Continuing the same therapy ignores signs of impending respiratory failure.
Rising PaCO₂ toward normal in a severely distressed asthmatic signals fatigue and impending failure, not improvement.
Asthma is not a fluid problem; diuretics have no role.

takeaway: In acute asthma, a normal or rising PaCO₂ with ongoing distress means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

stem: An intubated patient with severe COPD becomes hypotensive; the ventilator shows dynamic hyperinflation/auto-PEEP. Best immediate vent adjustment?

options.why: Faster rates and a 1:1 ratio shorten exhalation and worsen air trapping.

options.text: Decrease RR and increase expiratory time
options.why: Treat auto-PEEP by allowing more expiratory time; also treat bronchospasm and consider a brief circuit disconnect if crashing.
Larger volumes increase trapped air and intrathoracic pressure.

options.text: Add external PEEP equal to auto-PEEP
options.why: Matching external PEEP to auto-PEEP can ease triggering, but it does not relieve hyperinflation causing hypotension.

takeaway: For auto-PEEP with hypotension, lower the rate, shorten inspiratory time, and lengthen exhalation; disconnect briefly if crashing.

stem: A sudden rise in peak pressures with normal plateau pressures suggests:

options.why: Reduced compliance raises both peak and plateau pressures.
High peak with normal plateau = resistance problem (secretions, kink, bronchospasm). Suction, check tubing, and bronchodilate.
Pneumothorax reduces compliance, raising plateau as well as peak pressure.
Pulmonary edema stiffens the lung, raising plateau pressure.

takeaway: Peak up, plateau normal = airway resistance problem; peak and plateau both up = compliance problem.

stem: Post-line placement, patient acutely deteriorates, unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation. Best immediate action?

options.why: Waiting for a chest x-ray delays life-saving decompression.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; decompress immediately, then place a chest tube. Don't wait for imaging.
More PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure and worsens a tension pneumothorax.
Distended neck veins here reflect obstructed venous return, not fluid overload.

takeaway: Tension pneumothorax is treated with immediate needle decompression followed by a chest tube, without waiting for imaging.

stem: Minutes after a large thoracentesis, the patient suddenly develops pleuritic pain and dyspnea with decreased breath sounds on the tapped side. First action?

options.text: High-flow O₂ and notify provider—evaluate for pneumothorax
options.why: Sudden symptoms after thoracentesis suggest iatrogenic pneumothorax; give O₂ and arrange urgent confirmation and intervention.

options.text: Lay the patient flat and give fluids
options.why: Lying flat worsens dyspnea, and fluids do not address a pneumothorax.
Empyema develops over days, not minutes.
Incentive spirometry alone ignores a possible acute pneumothorax.

takeaway: New dyspnea and decreased breath sounds after thoracentesis suggest pneumothorax: give oxygen and notify the provider.

stem: Decompensated PH with RV failure and hypotension: which vasopressor is preferred?

options.why: Pure alpha-agonists raise pulmonary vascular resistance and can worsen RV afterload; avoid.
In RV failure from PH, norepinephrine supports MAP and coronary perfusion with less rise in PVR than pure alpha-agonists.
High-dose dopamine is arrhythmogenic and raises PVR; it is not preferred.
Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator and would worsen hypotension.

takeaway: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for hypotension in RV failure from pulmonary hypertension.

stem: Gold standard test for confirming pulmonary hypertension and tailoring therapy:

options.why: Echo estimates pulmonary pressures and screens for PH but cannot confirm it.
V/Q scanning screens for chronic thromboembolic PH but does not measure pressures.
Right heart catheterization is the gold standard to confirm PH and guide therapy, including vasoreactivity testing.
CTPA detects emboli but does not measure pulmonary artery pressure.

takeaway: Pulmonary hypertension is confirmed by right heart catheterization (mean PAP above 20 mmHg).

stem: Despite continuous β-agonists, steroids, and ipratropium, the patient remains tight with poor airflow. Evidence-based next therapy?

options.why: Evidence supports IV magnesium in status asthmaticus refractory to inhaled therapy to reduce bronchospasm.
Diuretics do not treat bronchospasm.
Hypertonic saline can provoke bronchospasm and is not an acute asthma therapy.
Most asthma exacerbations are not bacterial; antibiotics do not relieve bronchospasm.

takeaway: For severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and steroids, give IV magnesium sulfate.

stem: Fresh post-lobectomy, the chest tube is accidentally pulled out during transfer. Immediate nursing action?

options.text: Apply a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides, call the surgeon
options.why: For accidental chest-tube dislodgement, apply a three-sided occlusive dressing to prevent tension pneumothorax and notify the surgeon.

options.text: Leave the site open to the air
options.why: An open wound lets air enter the pleural space and collapse the lung.
The tube is already out; clamping does nothing, and waiting delays care.
Plain gauze allows air entry and does not seal the site.

takeaway: If a chest tube is pulled out, cover the site with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides and call the surgeon.

stem: Within 2 hours of transfusion, the patient develops acute hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, normal left-sided pressures, and no fluid overload. Best immediate step?

options.text: Stop transfusion; support oxygenation; notify blood bank
options.why: TRALI = acute non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours of transfusion; stop the transfusion, support oxygenation, and report to the blood bank. Diuretics are not helpful.
TRALI is not a volume problem; diuretics can worsen hypotension.
Vasodilators are not indicated and may worsen hypotension seen with TRALI.

options.text: Resume transfusion at a slower rate
options.why: Restarting the implicated product continues the injury.

takeaway: Suspected TRALI: stop the transfusion, support oxygenation (often like ARDS), and notify the blood bank.

stem: Which finding favors TACO over TRALI?

options.why: Hypotension favors TRALI; TACO usually causes hypertension.
TACO (volume overload) shows hypertension, elevated BNP, and cardiomegaly; TRALI tends to have normal BNP and may have hypotension.
Both TACO and TRALI occur within 6 hours, so timing does not distinguish them.
Both conditions cause bilateral infiltrates.

takeaway: TACO: hypertension, JVD, elevated BNP, responds to diuretics. TRALI: hypotension, normal BNP, no response to diuretics.

stem: A pneumonia patient on HFNC FiO₂ 0.9 remains SpO₂ 84%, appears exhausted, and is intermittently confused. Best next step?

options.text: Continue HFNC and recheck in 2 hours
options.why: Delaying intubation in a failing patient increases risk of arrest and mortality.
NIV is unsafe with confusion and inability to protect the airway, and is unlikely to fix refractory hypoxemia.
Persistent severe hypoxemia on maximal noninvasive support with fatigue and altered mental status = criteria for immediate airway control.
There is no sign of volume overload; diuretics would delay definitive airway management.

takeaway: Hypoxemia despite maximal noninvasive support plus fatigue or altered mental status requires intubation.

stem: An ARDS patient on VT 6 mL/kg PBW has plateaued at 32 cmH₂O. Best vent strategy adjustment now?

options.why: Larger volumes raise plateau pressure further and increase lung injury.

options.text: Decrease VT toward 4–5 mL/kg PBW and accept permissive hypercapnia
options.why: Lowering VT reduces plateau and driving pressure and ventilator-induced lung injury; permissive hypercapnia is accepted as long as pH is tolerated.
Removing PEEP causes alveolar collapse and worsens oxygenation.

options.text: Switch to pressure control with higher pressures
options.why: Higher pressures defeat the goal of keeping plateau 30 cmH₂O or less.

takeaway: If plateau pressure exceeds 30 cmH₂O at 6 mL/kg, reduce VT stepwise toward 4 mL/kg and accept permissive hypercapnia.

stem: A patient develops a 55% drop in platelets 6 days after starting heparin. They have new leg pain and swelling. What's the priority nursing action?

options.why: More heparin worsens HIT and its thrombotic complications.
Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in HIT because it can fuel thrombosis.

options.text: Stop all heparin products and notify the provider
options.why: Sudden platelet drop with thrombosis in a heparin-exposed patient = suspect HIT. Stop all heparin (including flushes) immediately and alert the provider.
Starting warfarin during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene; a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g., argatroban) is used first.

takeaway: Platelet drop of more than 50% 5–10 days after heparin, especially with thrombosis, is HIT: stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant.

stem: A patient develops SOB, crackles, HTN, and JVD during a transfusion. What's the most likely cause?

options.why: TRALI is non-cardiogenic and typically causes hypotension without JVD.
Classic signs of circulatory overload (hypertension, JVD, crackles) = TACO.
Acute hemolytic reaction causes fever, flank pain, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria.
Febrile reactions cause fever and chills without volume overload signs.

takeaway: Dyspnea, crackles, hypertension, and JVD during transfusion indicate TACO: stop or slow the transfusion and give diuretics.

stem: A cirrhotic patient presents with hematemesis, hypotension, and tachycardia. Which medication should the nurse anticipate administering first?

options.why: A PPI is helpful for ulcer bleeding but does not lower portal pressure in variceal bleeding.
Suspected variceal bleed: octreotide causes splanchnic vasoconstriction and reduces portal pressure.
Vitamin K acts slowly and does not stop active variceal hemorrhage.
Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy, not acute bleeding.

takeaway: In suspected variceal bleeding, start octreotide (plus antibiotic prophylaxis) and arrange urgent endoscopy.

stem: A patient is admitted with fever, hypotension, and altered mental status. Lactate is 5.1. Which order should the nurse prioritize?

options.why: Glucose control matters but is not the priority in sepsis-induced hypoperfusion.
Fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid within the first 3 hours) is the first-line intervention in sepsis-induced hypoperfusion.
Routine labs do not treat shock.
DVT prophylaxis is important later but is not an immediate resuscitation priority.

takeaway: Sepsis with hypotension or lactate of 4 mmol/L or more: give 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours along with cultures and early antibiotics.

stem: A patient with diabetes presents with a hot, swollen, and painful lower leg with red streaks and a temperature of 101.9°F. Which of the following should the nurse do first?

options.why: Cold compresses may ease discomfort but do not treat a spreading infection.
Immediate antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent progression to sepsis or deeper infection (obtain cultures first if systemic signs are present, without delaying therapy).

options.text: Mark the edge of erythema on the skin
options.why: Marking borders helps track spread but is a monitoring step and less urgent than starting antibiotics.

options.text: Prepare the patient for surgical debridement
options.why: Debridement is for necrotizing infection or abscess, which is not described here.

takeaway: Cellulitis with lymphangitic streaking and fever in a diabetic patient needs prompt antibiotics to prevent sepsis.

stem: A patient presents with severe leg pain after a minor cut 2 days ago. The exam reveals swelling, skin discoloration, crepitus, and hypotension. Which is the nurse's priority action?

options.why: Pain control matters but does not address the life-threatening infection.
Suspected necrotizing fasciitis requires urgent surgical debridement to prevent mortality.

options.text: Place the patient on NPO status
options.why: NPO prepares for surgery but is secondary to getting the surgical team involved.
Therapy is irrelevant in an acute surgical emergency.

takeaway: Pain out of proportion, crepitus, and shock after a minor wound suggest necrotizing fasciitis: emergency surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.

stem: A patient with DKA is admitted with a BG of 400 mg/dL and is receiving sliding scale insulin. What should the RN do next?

options.text: Continue sliding scale insulin as ordered
options.why: Subcutaneous sliding scale insulin is inadequate to close the anion gap in DKA.
Long-acting insulin alone does not provide the titratable insulin needed to reverse ketoacidosis.

options.text: Consult the physician about starting IV insulin infusion
options.why: DKA requires a continuous IV insulin infusion, not sliding scale subcutaneous insulin.
DKA patients are severely dehydrated and need aggressive IV fluids.

takeaway: Moderate-to-severe DKA is treated with IV fluids, potassium replacement, and a continuous IV insulin infusion.

stem: A patient with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (BG 836 mg/dL) is admitted for dehydration. Which additional lab values are expected?

options.why: Total-body potassium is depleted, but serum K is often normal or high at presentation; corrected sodium can be high, but the measured value is usually lowered by hyperglycemia.
Insulin deficiency causes potassium to shift out of cells; dilutional hyponatremia is common in HHS because glucose draws water into the vascular space.
Calcium and chloride changes are not characteristic of HHS.
Low bicarbonate with a high anion gap describes DKA; HHS has minimal ketosis and near-normal bicarbonate.

takeaway: In HHS, serum K may be normal or high despite total-body depletion, and measured Na is lowered by hyperglycemia (always calculate corrected sodium).
flag: Debatable key: measured Na is often low, but corrected Na is frequently normal to high in HHS from free-water loss, and serum K varies, so A is arguable.

stem: A primary concern in caring for a patient with pancreatitis is monitoring fluid and electrolytes closely because:

options.why: Fever adds to losses but is minor compared with third spacing.

options.text: Plasma volume is lost as enzymes increase capillary permeability
options.why: Pancreatitis leads to third spacing and hypovolemia from increased vascular permeability.
Vomiting can cause alkalosis, but it is not the main reason for close fluid monitoring.
AKI is a possible complication, not an expected outcome.

takeaway: Acute pancreatitis causes major third-spacing from capillary leak, so early fluid resuscitation and close monitoring are essential.

stem: Which laboratory profile is most consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?

options.why: DIC consumes platelets and raises split products; this is the opposite pattern.
DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy with fibrinolysis: prolonged clotting times, low platelets, and elevated fibrin split products and D-dimer.
A low D-dimer and high platelets argue against DIC.
Fibrinolysis in DIC raises, not lowers, split products and D-dimer.

takeaway: DIC labs: prolonged PT/PTT, low platelets and fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer and fibrin split products.

stem: The preferred laboratory to distinguish DKA from hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) is:

options.why: Ketones help, but the book keys osmolality; ketones alone do not capture HHS's defining hyperosmolarity.
HHS has markedly elevated osmolality (often above 320 mOsm/kg) with minimal ketosis, unlike DKA.
Chloride does not differentiate DKA from HHS.
Phosphorus may be abnormal in both and does not distinguish them.

takeaway: HHS: very high osmolality with little or no ketosis; DKA: ketosis with anion-gap acidosis.
flag: Debatable key: ketones, pH, and bicarbonate are the primary discriminators between DKA and HHS; osmolality supports HHS but can also be elevated in DKA.

stem: Abdominal distention, tympany, and high-pitched "tinkling" rushes coinciding with cramping most strongly indicate:

options.why: Peritonitis causes rigidity and rebound tenderness with hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.
Ileus causes distention with absent or diminished bowel sounds, not high-pitched rushes.
"Tinkling" high-pitched bowel sounds with colicky pain point to small bowel obstruction.
Ulcers cause epigastric pain, not distention with obstructive bowel sounds.

takeaway: High-pitched tinkling bowel sounds with colicky pain and distention suggest early mechanical small bowel obstruction.

stem: A patient with adrenal crisis: BP 74/40, Na⁺ 125, K⁺ 6.0, glucose 56. The best treatment is:

options.why: Adrenal crisis needs cortisol replacement (IV hydrocortisone), volume (normal saline), and correction of hypoglycemia; this also corrects hyperkalemia.
Vasopressors will not work well without cortisol replacement.
Diuretics worsen hypovolemia, and insulin worsens hypoglycemia.
Sedation has no role and would worsen hypotension.

takeaway: Adrenal crisis: give IV hydrocortisone, normal saline, and dextrose right away; do not delay steroids for testing.

stem: A patient with a crush injury to the thigh is admitted. Labs show CK of 60,000 U/L, potassium 6.2 mEq/L, and dark brown urine. What is the nurse’s priority intervention?

options.why: The patient is already hyperkalemic (6.2 mEq/L); giving potassium could precipitate a fatal dysrhythmia.
Fasciotomy treats compartment syndrome, which is not described here; the immediate threat is myoglobin-induced kidney injury.
High CK and dark urine = rhabdomyolysis; the primary goal is to preserve renal function via hydration and flush myoglobin through the kidneys.
Calcium stabilizes the myocardium if hyperkalemia causes ECG changes, but none are described; aggressive fluids address the underlying rhabdomyolysis.

takeaway: Rhabdomyolysis (very high CK, tea-colored urine) is treated first with aggressive IV fluids to prevent acute kidney injury.

stem: A patient with traumatic brain injury has an ICP of 24 mmHg and a MAP of 70 mmHg. Which action is most appropriate?

options.why: Head of bed is usually kept at about 30° to promote venous drainage; lowering to 15° does not address the low CPP.
Hypotonic fluids shift water into brain cells and worsen cerebral edema; hypertonic saline is used instead.
CPP = MAP – ICP = 70 – 24 = 46 mmHg, which is too low. Interventions should aim to raise MAP or lower ICP to keep CPP at least 60 mmHg.
Vigorous suctioning raises ICP; suctioning in TBI should be brief and preceded by oxygenation.

takeaway: CPP = MAP – ICP; in TBI keep CPP at about 60–70 mmHg and ICP below 22 mmHg.

stem: A cirrhotic patient presents with confusion, asterixis, and elevated ammonia. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Restrain the patient to prevent injury
options.why: Restraints do not treat the cause and can increase agitation and injury; they are a last resort.
Glucose does not lower ammonia; hypoglycemia should be checked, but it is not the treatment for hepatic encephalopathy.
Intubation is reserved for airway protection in grade 3–4 encephalopathy; this patient is confused but has no stated airway compromise.
Lactulose reduces ammonia levels by enhancing GI excretion, improving mental status in hepatic encephalopathy (Vilstrup et al., 2014).

takeaway: Lactulose (often with rifaximin) is first-line for hepatic encephalopathy; titrate to 2–3 soft stools per day.

stem: A patient with severe TBI has an ICP of 25 mmHg and a MAP of 70 mmHg. What is the calculated CPP and the priority action?

options.why: The CPP value is right, but with a high ICP and an EVD available, draining CSF lowers ICP directly and is the first-line step.

options.text: CPP = 55; Lower HOB to increase CPP
options.why: The calculation is wrong (70 – 25 = 45), and lowering the head of bed impairs venous drainage and can raise ICP.

options.text: CPP = 45; Drain CSF if EVD in place
options.why: CPP = 70 – 25 = 45 mmHg, which is low. If an EVD is available, draining CSF is first-line to reduce ICP and restore CPP.
The calculation is wrong (CPP is 45), and mannitol follows CSF drainage when an EVD is in place.

takeaway: With raised ICP and an EVD in place, CSF drainage is the fastest first-line way to lower ICP and improve CPP.

stem: A patient is post-op day 1 from a right-sided craniotomy for subdural hematoma evacuation. Which finding should be reported immediately?

options.why: Headache that responds to analgesics is expected after craniotomy.

options.text: Incision site oozing a small amount of blood
options.why: A small amount of oozing is common and is monitored, not an emergency.

options.text: GCS drops from 14 to 10 over 1 hour
options.why: An acute change in neuro status is a priority in post-craniotomy care and may indicate bleeding, herniation, or cerebral edema.
About 62 mL/hr is adequate urine output (more than 0.5 mL/kg/hr).

takeaway: A GCS drop of 2 or more points after neurosurgery is an emergency until proven otherwise; report it immediately.

stem: A patient presents with head trauma, followed by a lucid period and then rapid deterioration. CT shows a lens-shaped bleed. What is the likely diagnosis?

options.why: Subdural hematomas are venous, appear crescent-shaped on CT, and usually develop more slowly.
SAH presents with a sudden severe ("thunderclap") headache and blood in the basal cisterns, not a lens-shaped collection.

Epidural hematoma typically follows head trauma with a brief lucid interval before rapid deterioration. It most often involves arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery and appears lens-shaped (biconvex) on CT.
ICH is bleeding within the brain tissue itself, usually hypertensive, and does not have a classic lucid interval or lens shape.

takeaway: Lucid interval + lens-shaped (biconvex) bleed = epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery; needs emergent surgery.

stem: A 74-year-old patient on mechanical ventilation has become increasingly drowsy and inattentive over the past 12 hours. The nurse notes no agitation or restlessness. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.why: Antipsychotics are not first-line and are not indicated for hypoactive delirium without severe agitation.
Hypoactive delirium is common and often missed. Early screening with a validated tool (CAM-ICU) allows prompt intervention.
Deeper sedation worsens delirium and prolongs ventilation; the patient is already drowsy.
The patient is not agitated, and restraints increase delirium risk; they are not an assessment step.

takeaway: Drowsy, inattentive ICU patients may have hypoactive delirium; screen with CAM-ICU before any drug or sedation change.

stem: An ICU patient recovering from ARDS reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, and poor appetite for the past month. The nurse’s priority is to:

options.why: Reassurance alone skips the safety assessment and may minimize a serious depressive episode.
Safety is the priority. Depression in ICU patients carries increased suicide risk; screening and immediate safety measures come before activity promotion or delayed referral.

options.text: Request a psychiatric consultation after discharge
options.why: Delaying evaluation until discharge leaves a possible safety risk unaddressed now.

options.text: Suggest an antidepressant to the provider
options.why: Medication may be appropriate later, but assessing suicide risk comes first.

takeaway: With signs of depression, assess for suicidal ideation first; safety comes before other interventions.

stem: A 54-year-old male with a history of alcohol use disorder is admitted to the ICU after a GI bleed. Twelve hours later, he develops tremors, agitation, and diaphoresis. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

options.why: In alcohol withdrawal, thiamine must be given before glucose to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; it does not treat alcohol withdrawal and can provoke seizures.

options.text: Place patient in restraints to prevent injury
options.why: Restraints worsen agitation and do not treat withdrawal.

options.text: Administer naloxone for suspected opioid overdose
options.why: Naloxone is for opioid overdose; tremors, agitation, and diaphoresis 12 hours after the last drink suggest alcohol withdrawal.

takeaway: In alcohol withdrawal: thiamine before glucose, benzodiazepines for symptoms, and monitor for DTs at 48–72 hours.

stem: A patient is admitted after being found unresponsive with shallow respirations and pinpoint pupils. What is the priority intervention?

options.why: Classic triad of opioid overdose = pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, ↓ LOC. Naloxone is the immediate reversal agent.
Lorazepam is for alcohol- or stimulant-related agitation and would further depress respirations.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and pinpoint pupils point to opioids; it also carries a seizure risk.

options.text: Encourage the patient to drink fluids
options.why: The patient is unresponsive; oral fluids risk aspiration and do not treat overdose.

takeaway: Pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + ↓ LOC = opioid overdose; support ventilation and give naloxone, then watch for re-sedation.

stem: A patient presents with chest pain, severe hypertension, and agitation after cocaine use. Which intervention should the nurse avoid?

options.why: Benzodiazepines are first-line for cocaine toxicity; they reduce agitation, heart rate, and blood pressure.
Nitroglycerin relieves coronary vasospasm and chest pain in cocaine toxicity and is appropriate.
Beta-blockers (like labetalol, propranolol) are avoided in acute cocaine toxicity due to unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation → worsening vasospasm.
A quiet environment reduces sympathetic stimulation and is appropriate.

takeaway: In acute cocaine toxicity use benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin; avoid beta-blockers because of unopposed alpha stimulation.

stem: A 65-year-old patient with COPD presents with somnolence, PaO₂ 54 mmHg, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, and pH 7.28. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.why: Bicarbonate does not fix hypoventilation; the acidosis is respiratory, so the solution is to improve ventilation.

options.text: Increase oxygen to 100% with non-rebreather mask
options.why: Too much O₂ in COPD can worsen CO₂ retention, and oxygen alone does not correct hypoventilation.

options.text: Assist ventilation with BiPAP or intubation
options.why: Respiratory acidosis (↑CO₂, ↓pH) = hypoventilation. The solution is to improve ventilation with noninvasive or invasive support.
A somnolent patient cannot reliably follow coaching, and it will not reverse acute hypercapnic failure.

takeaway: Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis in COPD is treated by supporting ventilation (BiPAP, or intubation if obtunded), not bicarbonate.

stem: A post-op patient with prolonged NG suction has ABGs: pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 45, HCO₃⁻ 32. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely present?

options.why: Gastric losses and alkalosis drive potassium into cells and out in urine, lowering, not raising, potassium.
Metabolic alkalosis commonly coexists with hypokalemia and hypochloremia due to gastric losses (and diuretics).
NG losses tend to lower magnesium; hypermagnesemia is seen with renal failure or excess intake.
Sodium may change, but the classic pairing with NG-suction metabolic alkalosis is hypokalemia.

takeaway: Prolonged NG suction or vomiting → metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia and hypochloremia.

stem: A patient with AKI has peaked T waves on ECG, K⁺ = 7.2 mEq/L. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate first?

options.why: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane → prevents fatal arrhythmias. It is the first step when hyperkalemia causes ECG changes.
Loop diuretics lower potassium slowly and may not work in AKI; they do not protect the heart now.
Bicarbonate shifts potassium only modestly and is mainly used with metabolic acidosis; it does not stabilize the myocardium.
Dialysis removes potassium definitively but takes time to set up; the heart must be protected first.

takeaway: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: calcium first (protect the heart), then shift (insulin/glucose), then remove (dialysis, binders, diuretics).

stem: A septic patient’s ABG shows: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 37, HCO₃⁻ 18. What is the primary acid–base imbalance?

options.why: Respiratory acidosis requires a PaCO₂ above 45 mmHg; here PaCO₂ is normal.
Low pH, low HCO₃⁻ with normal CO₂ = metabolic acidosis (commonly from lactic acidosis in sepsis).
The pH is acidotic and PaCO₂ is not low, so this is not an alkalosis.
The pH of 7.30 is acidotic, which rules out any alkalosis as the primary disorder.

takeaway: pH low + HCO₃⁻ low = metabolic acidosis; in sepsis think lactic acidosis.

stem: A post-thyroidectomy patient develops twitching, stridor, and positive Chvostek’s sign. Which intervention is most urgent?

options.why: Acute hypocalcemia (from parathyroid injury) → tetany and airway compromise. Immediate IV calcium replacement is lifesaving.
Seizure precautions are reasonable, but they do not correct the cause or relieve the laryngospasm causing stridor.
Fluid restriction has no role in hypocalcemia and does not address the airway threat.
Breathing exercises will not relieve laryngospasm from hypocalcemia.

takeaway: Stridor, tetany, and Chvostek’s sign after thyroidectomy = acute hypocalcemia; give IV calcium gluconate immediately.

stem: A kidney transplant recipient, 5 days post-op, develops fever, rising creatinine, decreased urine output, and tenderness over the graft site. Which complication is most likely?

options.why: Hyperacute rejection is antibody-mediated and occurs within minutes to hours of reperfusion, not days later.
Acute rejection occurs days to weeks post-transplant and is T-cell mediated, presenting with fever, graft tenderness, rising creatinine, and falling urine output.
Chronic rejection develops gradually over months to years.
Cyclosporine toxicity causes renal dysfunction but not fever or graft tenderness.

takeaway: Fever + graft tenderness + rising creatinine days to weeks after transplant = acute (T-cell) rejection.

stem: A patient 2 days after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass has HR 128, fever 100.8°F, and severe abdominal pain. Which action is most important?

options.why: Treating fever masks the problem without addressing a possible leak.

options.text: Encourage ambulation to relieve gas pain
options.why: Assuming gas pain delays recognition of a life-threatening complication.
Tachycardia is the earliest sign of an anastomotic leak, a life-threatening complication that requires immediate surgical evaluation.
There is no nausea described, and antiemetics do not address the likely leak.

takeaway: After bariatric surgery, unexplained tachycardia (HR above 120) is an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise; notify the surgeon.

stem: A patient who had a gastric bypass reports dizziness, palpitations, and diarrhea 20 minutes after eating. Which dietary teaching is most appropriate?

options.why: Large, high-carbohydrate meals worsen dumping syndrome.

options.text: Avoid protein and fat to prevent delayed emptying
options.why: Protein and some fat slow gastric emptying and help prevent dumping; they should not be avoided.

options.text: Eat small, frequent meals, high protein, low carb
options.why: Small, frequent, high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals prevent dumping syndrome.

options.text: Drink plenty of fluids with meals to aid digestion
options.why: Consuming fluids with meals accelerates gastric emptying; fluids should be taken between meals.

takeaway: Dumping syndrome: small frequent meals, high protein, low simple carbohydrate, and fluids between (not with) meals.

stem: A trauma patient presents with HR 132, BP 80/40, cool, clammy skin, and UOP <15 mL/hr. CVP is 2 mmHg, CO is 3.0 L/min, and SVR is elevated. What is the priority intervention?

options.why: Vasopressors are ineffective without preload; the tank must be filled first.
Classic hypovolemic shock (↓ preload, ↑ SVR, ↓ CO). Volume replacement with fluids/blood products is first-line.

options.text: Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position
options.why: Trendelenburg gives little sustained benefit and can impair ventilation; it is not a substitute for volume.
Acidosis from hypoperfusion is corrected by restoring perfusion, not bicarbonate.

takeaway: Low CVP + low CO + high SVR = hypovolemic shock; restore volume (blood products in hemorrhage) before vasopressors.
flag: Keyed answer is the best option, but in hemorrhagic trauma current ATLS practice limits crystalloid (about 1 L) and prioritizes early blood products; 30 mL/kg crystalloid is the sepsis dose.

stem: A patient in distributive shock is noted to have hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Which hemodynamic pattern best describes this state?

options.why: High SVR, low CO and high preload describe cardiogenic shock.
Distributive shock is defined by low, not high, SVR.
Preload is not elevated in distributive shock, and CO is usually normal or high early.
Distributive shock (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) = hallmark ↓ SVR due to vasodilation, with CO normal/high early and preload low.

takeaway: Distributive shock: ↓ SVR (vasodilation), normal or ↑ CO early, ↓ preload.
flag: Minor inconsistency: stem says fluid resuscitation was adequate, yet the keyed pattern lists ↓ preload. Key is still the best match for distributive shock.

stem: An ICU patient with sepsis has a fever of 103°F, HR 120, BP 90/50, bounding pulses, and warm, flushed skin. Which best explains these findings?

options.why: Preload is typically low, not high, in septic vasodilation.
Early/warm septic shock = low SVR (vasodilation) with high/normal CO → bounding pulses and warm skin.
High SVR and low CO produce cool, clammy skin and weak pulses, the opposite of this picture.
Low CO would cause weak pulses and cool skin, not bounding pulses and flushing.

takeaway: Warm septic shock = low SVR with high/normal CO, giving warm flushed skin and bounding pulses.

stem: Which of the following is included in the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 1-hour bundle?

options.why: Vasopressors are started when hypotension persists during or after fluid resuscitation, not routinely before fluids.
Antibiotics should be given within 1 hour after cultures are drawn; waiting for results delays treatment.

options.text: Measure lactate, draw cultures, give antibiotics, give 30 mL/kg crystalloids
options.why: Within 1 hour: lactate, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L.

options.text: Use dopamine as a first-line vasopressor
options.why: Norepinephrine, not dopamine, is the first-line vasopressor if MAP is below 65 mmHg.

takeaway: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate, cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid if hypotensive, and norepinephrine for MAP below 65.

stem: A patient with sepsis now presents with hypotension, mottled cool extremities, weak pulses, and AMS despite fluids. Which therapy is most appropriate?

options.why: Dopamine is no longer first-line in septic shock because it causes more dysrhythmias than norepinephrine.
Shock persisting despite fluids needs a vasopressor; norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor to restore MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
Hypotension has persisted despite fluids; more fluid alone risks overload without restoring perfusion.
Fever control does not treat hypotension or poor perfusion.

takeaway: Septic shock with hypotension despite fluids: start norepinephrine, targeting MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
flag: Book rationale describes late/cold septic shock as low SVR + low CO; cold shock usually shows falling CO with rising SVR. The keyed answer (norepinephrine) is correct.

stem: A patient presents after a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose. ECG shows QRS widening and ventricular dysrhythmias. Which treatment is most appropriate?

options.why: Naloxone reverses opioids and has no effect on TCA sodium-channel blockade.
N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen toxicity.
TCA toxicity causes QRS widening and lethal arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures in TCA overdose.

takeaway: TCA overdose with QRS widening → IV sodium bicarbonate.

stem: A trauma patient is admitted with a core temperature of 32°C (89.6°F), bradycardia, hypotension, and coagulopathy. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.why: Cooling blankets would worsen hypothermia.
Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia, not hypothermia.
This is moderate hypothermia. Active rewarming (warm blankets, warmed fluids, heated humidified O₂) is the priority.
Acetaminophen lowers temperature and would worsen hypothermia.

takeaway: Hypothermia in trauma worsens coagulopathy (part of the lethal triad); actively rewarm moderate hypothermia (28–32°C).

stem: A patient with end-stage COPD, alert and oriented, refuses mechanical ventilation despite family insistence. What is the nurse’s best action?

options.text: Encourage the family to override the patient’s wishes
options.why: Family cannot override a competent patient’s refusal of treatment.

options.text: Respect the patient’s decision and notify the care team
options.why: Autonomy is a patient’s right to make decisions about their own care. Family cannot override a competent patient’s refusal.
Starting ventilation against a competent patient’s refusal violates autonomy and informed consent.

options.text: Request an ethics consult to force treatment
options.why: Ethics consultation supports decision-making; it cannot be used to force treatment on a competent patient.

takeaway: A competent patient’s informed refusal is honored even when the family disagrees.

stem: A patient is ventilated with no chance of meaningful recovery. The family elects to withdraw life support. What is the nurse’s role?

options.text: Explain that withdrawing care is the same as euthanasia
options.why: Withdrawal of life support is ethically and legally distinct from euthanasia; saying otherwise is inaccurate and harmful.
Withdrawal ≠ euthanasia. The nurse ensures comfort and dignity at the end of life, supporting both the patient and their family.

options.text: Remove the ventilator without physician's order
options.why: Withdrawal requires a provider order and a coordinated plan.

options.text: Decline participation due to ethical conflict
options.why: Conscientious objection requires a hand-off arranged in advance; declining does not meet the patient’s needs at this moment.

takeaway: Withdrawing life support is not euthanasia; the nurse’s focus is comfort, dignity, and family support.

stem: During a mass casualty incident, one ventilator is available for three critically ill patients. Which ethical principle guides the allocation of this resource?

options.why: Autonomy concerns an individual’s right to self-determination, not how scarce resources are distributed.
Nonmaleficence means avoiding harm; it does not decide fair distribution among patients.
Justice = fairness in distributing resources. Triage decisions are guided by justice.
Beneficence means doing good for an individual patient; allocation among several patients is a matter of justice.

takeaway: Allocation of scarce resources (triage) is guided by justice.

stem: A nurse is caring for a patient with multi-organ failure who is not responding to maximal therapy. The family insists on “doing everything” despite the patient’s prior wishes for comfort care only. The nurse feels increasingly anxious and morally conflicted. This scenario best describes:

options.why: Burnout is cumulative exhaustion from workload and work environment, not distress tied to a specific ethical conflict.
Compassion fatigue is secondary trauma from exposure to suffering, not conflict over what is ethically right.
Moral distress occurs when a nurse knows the ethically appropriate action but feels powerless to act due to external constraints (family, providers, system).
The nurse has not acted unethically; they are experiencing distress about the situation.

takeaway: Moral distress = knowing the right action but being constrained from taking it.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step for a nurse experiencing moral distress about providing non-beneficial care?

options.why: Refusing without a hand-off abandons the patient and skips available resources.

options.text: Request a transfer to another unit
options.why: Transferring avoids the problem rather than addressing it.

options.text: Discuss concerns with the charge nurse or ethics committee
options.why: Open communication with leadership or ethics resources is the first step in addressing moral distress before escalation.
Going straight to administration bypasses the chain of command and the ethics resources meant for this.

takeaway: Address moral distress first through the charge nurse, chain of command, or ethics committee.

stem: A patient with advanced cancer has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. During a rapid response event, the patient becomes pulseless. The physician orders CPR. What is the nurse’s best action?

options.why: Starting CPR without addressing the documented DNR could violate the patient’s expressed wishes.

options.text: Clarify the code status before initiating CPR
options.why: Advocacy requires ensuring the patient’s expressed wishes (DNR) are honored, even during emergencies; the conflict must be resolved immediately.

options.text: Refuse to participate and leave the room
options.why: Leaving abandons the patient and does not resolve the conflict.

options.text: Wait for the ethics committee to decide
options.why: An ethics committee cannot convene during an arrest; the question must be clarified on the spot.

takeaway: When an order conflicts with a documented DNR, immediately clarify code status with the provider; the patient’s wishes guide care.

stem: A nurse is assigned to care for a patient on life support whose family wants aggressive care, though the patient’s advance directive states no extraordinary measures. Which principle should guide the nurse’s advocacy?

options.why: Beneficence (doing good) matters, but here the decision rests on honoring the patient’s own stated wishes.
Avoiding harm is relevant, but the core issue is the patient’s right to self-determination.
Patient autonomy, the right to self-determination, takes precedence and requires honoring the patient’s advance directive.
Justice concerns fair distribution of resources, not whose wishes guide this patient’s care.

takeaway: An advance directive is an expression of autonomy and takes precedence over family preference.

stem: A patient is declared brain-dead and is a registered organ donor. The family is distraught and requests withdrawal of all interventions without organ donation. What is the nurse’s best immediate action?

options.text: Respect the family’s wishes and stop care
options.why: Stopping support before OPO involvement could forfeit the patient’s documented donation decision.
Federal regulations require timely referral to the OPO, and only the OPO (or its trained requestors) approaches families about donation; the nurse notifies the OPO first.
Extubating without an order or OPO involvement is inappropriate.

options.text: Delay action until the ethics committee meets
options.why: Waiting delays the required OPO referral and may compromise organ viability.

takeaway: For any death or imminent death, notify the OPO; the OPO, not the bedside nurse, discusses donation with the family.

stem: A Muslim patient in the ICU is scheduled for surgery during Ramadan. The patient expresses concern about fasting. What is the most culturally sensitive nursing action?

options.text: Encourage the patient to break the fast for health reasons
options.why: Pressuring the patient dismisses their religious practice; the decision should come from the patient.

options.text: Notify the dietary to hold meals until sundown
options.why: Respecting fasting practices while ensuring health needs are met is a culturally sensitive approach. Always involve patient preference in care planning.

options.text: Offer IV fluids during fasting hours without discussing with the patient
options.why: Acting without discussion ignores the patient’s preferences and consent.

options.text: Explain that hospital policy overrides fasting practices
options.why: This dismisses the patient’s beliefs and is not culturally sensitive.

takeaway: Accommodate religious practices such as fasting whenever safe, and plan care with the patient.

stem: A patient with limited English proficiency is about to sign a surgical consent. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Ask a bilingual family member to translate
options.why: Family translators risk misinterpretation, omissions, and bias.
Certified interpreters ensure accurate, ethical communication for informed consent.

options.text: Simplify medical terms and repeat them
options.why: Simplifying English does not overcome a language barrier.

options.text: Proceed with consent since the patient nods in agreement
options.why: Nodding does not show understanding; consent would not be informed.

takeaway: Informed consent for a patient with limited English proficiency requires a certified medical interpreter, not family.

stem: A nurse notices their own frustration when caring for a patient whose cultural practices delay treatment. Which professional behavior demonstrates cultural sensitivity?

options.text: Ignoring the practices to complete care quickly
options.why: Ignoring the patient’s practices disrespects them and can damage trust.

options.text: Asking another nurse to take over
options.why: Handing off avoids the nurse’s own bias rather than addressing it.

options.text: Reflecting on personal bias and adapting care respectfully
options.why: Self-awareness and adaptation are key to cultural sensitivity and professional caring practice.

options.text: Explaining to the patient why cultural practices are unsafe
options.why: Labeling the practices unsafe without assessment is judgmental and not culturally sensitive.

takeaway: Cultural sensitivity starts with recognizing one’s own biases and adapting care respectfully.

stem: An experienced ICU nurse feels emotionally drained and detached after multiple patient deaths. What is the nurse most likely experiencing?

options.why: Burnout stems mainly from workload and the work environment rather than repeated exposure to patient suffering and death.
Compassion fatigue is secondary trauma from patient suffering, leading to emotional exhaustion and detachment.
Moral resilience is the ability to recover from ethical challenges, not a state of exhaustion.
Depression is a clinical diagnosis requiring more criteria; this picture fits a work-related reaction to repeated loss.

takeaway: Emotional exhaustion and detachment after repeated patient suffering or death = compassion fatigue.

stem: Which action best supports the prevention of compassion fatigue among ICU nurses?

options.text: Increasing overtime shifts to build resilience
options.why: More overtime increases exhaustion and risk of compassion fatigue.

options.text: Participating in debriefing sessions after traumatic events
options.why: Debriefing and peer support are evidence-based strategies to reduce compassion fatigue.

options.text: Suppressing emotional responses to patient loss
options.why: Suppressing emotions increases distress over time.
Avoidance is not sustainable in the ICU and does not build coping.

takeaway: Debriefing and peer support after traumatic events help prevent compassion fatigue.

stem: A nurse describes feeling overwhelmed by repeated trauma exposure and is considering leaving the ICU. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Recommend immediate transfer to another unit
options.why: Transfer may be considered later, but it is avoidance and does not provide support.

options.text: Provide peer and counseling support resources
options.why: Compassion fatigue requires acknowledgment, peer support, and mental health resources, not avoidance.

options.text: Suggest ignoring the feelings until they resolve
options.why: Ignoring the feelings allows distress to worsen.

options.text: Encourage the nurse to take on fewer critical patients
options.why: Reducing acuity alone does not address the emotional impact.

takeaway: Respond to compassion fatigue with acknowledgment, peer support, and counseling/EAP resources.

stem: A patient is being compassionately extubated. What is the nurse’s priority action?

options.why: High-flow oxygen is not routinely needed for comfort and does not relieve air hunger the way opioids do.

options.text: Administer opioid analgesics and anxiolytics as ordered
options.why: Priority is patient comfort. Sedation and analgesia are essential before terminal extubation.

options.text: Explain the process to the family after extubation
options.why: The family should be prepared before extubation, not after.

options.text: Withhold sedation to assess patient comfort
options.why: Withholding medication risks distress and air hunger.

takeaway: Before compassionate (terminal) extubation, give opioids and anxiolytics to prevent air hunger and distress.

stem: Which intervention best maintains dignity during end-of-life care?

options.text: Avoiding family involvement to prevent conflict
options.why: Excluding the family removes support and disregards patient and family wishes.

options.text: Continuing all invasive procedures until death
options.why: Unnecessary invasive procedures cause suffering without benefit.

options.text: Maintaining privacy, respect, and honoring patient wishes
options.why: Dignity is preserved by respecting wishes, avoiding unnecessary procedures, and maintaining privacy.

options.text: Prioritizing nurse convenience over patient preference
options.why: Care is centered on the patient, not on staff convenience.

takeaway: Dignity at end of life = privacy, respect, and honoring the patient’s wishes.

stem: The family asks how to know their loved one is comfortable at the end of life. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: “We will monitor for pain, anxiety, and provide medications to keep them comfortable.”
options.why: Honest reassurance with active symptom management is key in end-of-life communication.

options.text: “It is natural to suffer at the end of life, but we minimize it when possible.”
options.why: This normalizes suffering and may increase family distress.

options.text: “Most patients do not feel pain during the dying process.”
options.why: This is false reassurance; many dying patients need active symptom management.

options.text: “Your loved one won’t need medications unless they ask.”
options.why: Dying patients often cannot ask; comfort is assessed with behavioral cues and treated proactively.

takeaway: Reassure families honestly and describe active monitoring and treatment of pain and anxiety.

stem: A dying patient with advanced COPD is anxious and dyspneic. What is the best nursing intervention?

options.why: Oxygen helps only if hypoxemic and does not relieve the sensation of dyspnea as well as opioids do.

options.text: Administer opioids for dyspnea and anxiety relief
options.why: Opioids are evidence-based for relieving dyspnea and anxiety in end-of-life care, even in COPD. Comfort takes priority over concern for respiratory depression.

options.text: Perform frequent suctioning to keep the airway clear
options.why: Frequent suctioning is uncomfortable and does not relieve dyspnea without secretions.

options.text: Withhold medication to avoid respiratory depression
options.why: Withholding leaves the patient suffering; appropriately titrated opioids are safe and indicated at end of life.

takeaway: At end of life, opioids are first-line for dyspnea, even in COPD.

stem: An 82-year-old ICU patient is receiving morphine for pain. Which consideration is most important for this age group?

options.text: They require higher opioid doses due to tolerance
options.why: Older adults usually need lower, not higher, opioid doses.

options.text: Slower metabolism and renal clearance may increase toxicity
options.why: Older adults have altered pharmacokinetics, necessitating careful dose adjustments to prevent accumulation and adverse effects (morphine metabolites are renally cleared).

options.text: Elderly patients rarely experience opioid side effects
options.why: Older adults are more, not less, prone to sedation, respiratory depression, and delirium from opioids.

options.text: Pain perception decreases significantly in older adults
options.why: Pain is often under-treated in older adults because of this myth; pain perception is not reliably reduced.

takeaway: Start low and go slow with opioids in older adults; reduced renal clearance lets morphine metabolites accumulate.

stem: A 14-year-old ICU patient requires a central line placement. Which nursing action best reflects age-appropriate care?

options.text: Only explaining the procedure to the parents
options.why: Adolescents should be included in explanations and decisions about their own care.

options.text: Using play therapy or simple language to reduce fear
options.why: Adolescents need clear, age-appropriate explanations and involvement in care decisions; distraction reduces anxiety.
Family and peer support help adolescents cope; restricting visits increases anxiety.

options.text: Avoiding involvement of the patient in care decisions
options.why: Adolescents value independence and should be involved in their care.

takeaway: Adolescents need honest, clear explanations, privacy, and involvement in their own care decisions.
flag: Play therapy is mainly for younger children; for a 14-year-old the best part of the keyed option is clear, simple explanation. Key is still the best option given.

stem: A nurse is caring for a 40-year-old patient recovering from an MI who is anxious about returning to work and supporting their family. Which nursing intervention best reflects age-appropriate care?

options.text: Focus care only on physiologic recovery
options.why: Ignoring psychosocial stressors misses a key need of middle-aged adults and can affect recovery.

options.text: Include psychosocial stressors in discharge planning
options.why: Age-appropriate care encompasses both physiological recovery and psychosocial aspects, including employment and family support.
Delaying teaching leaves the patient unprepared for discharge; teaching should be adapted, not postponed.
Teaching limited to physical restrictions misses the work and family concerns the patient raised.

takeaway: Care for middle-aged adults includes work, financial, and family-role stressors in discharge planning.

stem: A Spanish-speaking patient with limited English proficiency is scheduled for surgery. What is the nurse’s priority?

options.why: Professional interpreters ensure safe and ethical communication; family members are not always reliable or appropriate.

options.text: Asking the patient’s child to interpret
options.why: Using a child is inappropriate and risks errors, omissions, and burden on the child.
Gestures cannot convey the information needed for safe surgical care and consent.
Nodding does not show understanding.

takeaway: Use certified medical interpreters, never children or untrained family, for patients with limited English proficiency.

stem: A Muslim female patient requests a female nurse for catheterization. Which nursing response is most culturally competent?

options.text: Explain that staffing does not allow accommodations
options.why: Refusing without trying dismisses a reasonable cultural and religious request.

options.text: Honor the request and assign a female nurse if possible
options.why: Respecting cultural values about gender preferences demonstrates cultural competence and dignity in care.

options.text: Educate the patient that gender preference is unnecessary
options.why: This dismisses the patient’s values and is not culturally competent.

options.text: Delay the procedure until the patient accepts any nurse
options.why: Delaying care to pressure the patient is coercive and may cause harm.

takeaway: Honor gender-of-caregiver requests whenever possible as part of culturally competent, dignified care.

stem: A patient’s cultural belief conflicts with a recommended treatment plan. Which action demonstrates cultural competence?

options.text: Ignore the belief and implement the treatment
options.why: Ignoring the belief disregards autonomy and damages trust.

options.text: Negotiate a care plan that integrates cultural values with safe practice
options.why: Cultural competence means collaboration: acknowledging beliefs while ensuring patient safety (the LEARN model).

options.text: Inform the patient that cultural beliefs are not medically valid
options.why: Dismissing beliefs is disrespectful and harms the relationship.

options.text: Ask another nurse to take the assignment
options.why: Handing off avoids the issue rather than resolving it.

takeaway: Use the LEARN model (Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate) to blend cultural values with safe care.

stem: Which example reflects a health inequity in critical care?

options.why: Developing ARDS is a clinical event, not by itself an avoidable, unfair difference in care.

options.text: A patient is unable to access follow-up care due to a lack of insurance
options.why: This represents a health inequity: an avoidable barrier rooted in socioeconomic disadvantage.

options.text: A patient develops delirium after sedation
options.why: Delirium is a clinical complication, not a social or economic disparity.

options.text: A patient experiences sepsis after surgery
options.why: Postoperative sepsis is a complication, not an inequity in access or outcome.

takeaway: Health inequities are unfair, avoidable differences caused by social or economic disadvantage, such as lack of insurance.

stem: A patient from a low-income background misses follow-up appointments due to lack of transportation. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.why: Labeling the patient noncompliant ignores the real barrier.

options.text: Refer to social services for transportation resources
options.why: Addressing social determinants (transportation) promotes equitable access and continuity of care.
Discharging without addressing the barrier leaves the patient at risk.

options.text: Advise the patient to borrow money for taxis
options.why: This is impractical and shifts the burden back to the patient.

takeaway: Screen for social determinants of health and refer to social work or case management to remove barriers.

stem: In the ICU, minority patients with sepsis show higher mortality rates compared to other groups. Which nursing role best addresses this inequity?

options.why: Ignoring disparities allows them to continue.

options.text: Advocating for equitable access to evidence-based sepsis protocols
options.why: The nurse advocates for fairness and justice, ensuring all patients receive guideline-based care regardless of their demographics.

options.text: Explaining disparities are due to genetics
options.why: Attributing disparities to genetics ignores social and system causes and is inaccurate.

options.text: Delaying interventions until disparities are studied further
options.why: Delaying evidence-based care worsens outcomes.

takeaway: Nurses address disparities by advocating for consistent, guideline-based care for every patient (justice).

stem: A hospital identifies language barriers delaying care for non-English-speaking patients. Which system-level nursing intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Train staff to avoid using interpreters
options.why: This would worsen communication and safety.

options.text: Establish interpreter services and multilingual resources
options.why: System-level action ensures equity and reduces delays in care for patients with language barriers.

options.text: Ask bilingual family members to routinely translate
options.why: Routine family interpretation is unreliable and inappropriate.

options.text: Focus resources only on English-speaking patients
options.why: This is discriminatory and violates justice.

takeaway: System-level fixes for language barriers: professional interpreter services and multilingual materials.

stem: A patient in the ICU is in septic shock. The family is overwhelmed and tearful. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Provide short, honest updates in simple language
options.why: Families in crisis benefit from clarity, honesty, and simplified communication.

options.text: Avoid updates until the patient stabilizes
options.why: Withholding updates increases anxiety and erodes trust.

options.text: Use medical terms so the family understands clinical accuracy
