options.why: When a provider will not change an unsafe prescription, the nurse withholds the drug and follows the chain of command to protect the client.

takeaway: Never give a medication you believe is unsafe; withhold it and go up the chain of command.

stem: The nurse finds a client sitting on the floor beside the bed. The client says, "I slipped trying to get to the bathroom." After assessing the client and notifying the provider, which documentation action is correct?

options.text: Complete an incident report with objective facts, and document the assessment in the medical record without mentioning the incident report.
options.why: The incident report is a confidential quality-improvement tool; the chart contains the factual assessment and care but no reference to the report.

options.text: Write "incident report completed" in the client's progress notes.
options.why: Referencing the incident report in the chart can make it part of the legal record and discoverable; it should not be mentioned.

options.text: Place a copy of the incident report in the client's medical record.
options.why: Incident reports are kept separate from the medical record and are filed according to facility policy.

options.text: Record in the incident report that the client fell because the UAP did not answer the call light.
options.why: Incident reports contain objective facts (for example, "client found sitting on floor" and the client's own words), not opinions or blame.

takeaway: Incident reports: objective facts only, no blame, never placed in or mentioned in the client's chart.

stem: The nurse brings a surgical consent form to a client scheduled for a mastectomy. The client says, "I'm not sure whether the surgeon is going to remove my lymph nodes too." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain the lymph node procedure to the client and then witness the signature.
options.why: Explaining the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives is the surgeon's responsibility, not the nurse's.

options.text: Have the client sign the form because the operating room is ready.
options.why: Consent signed without understanding is not informed consent; schedule pressure does not change that.

options.text: Hold the consent form and notify the surgeon that the client needs more information.
options.why: The nurse's role is to confirm understanding and witness the signature; when the client is not fully informed, the nurse stops and notifies the surgeon.

options.text: Ask the client's spouse to sign the consent on the client's behalf.
options.why: A competent adult client signs their own consent; a spouse cannot sign for a client who has decision-making capacity.

takeaway: The provider obtains informed consent; the nurse witnesses the signature and notifies the provider if the client does not understand.

stem: The charge nurse hears two UAPs arguing loudly in the hallway about who should care for a client who needs total assistance. What is the charge nurse's best initial action?

options.text: Tell both UAPs to stop and assign the client to the one with fewer clients.
options.why: An authoritarian decision ends the argument but does not address the cause and may leave lasting conflict.

options.text: Ask both UAPs to move to a private area and discuss the issue with each of them.
options.why: Moving the conflict out of public view protects clients and privacy, and hearing both sides allows a collaborative (win-win) solution.

options.text: Report both UAPs to the nurse manager for unprofessional behavior.
options.why: Escalating before trying to resolve the conflict at the unit level skips an appropriate first step.

options.text: Ignore the disagreement so the UAPs can work it out themselves.
options.why: Avoidance leaves the conflict unresolved and allows it to affect client care.

takeaway: Address staff conflict early, privately, and collaboratively; avoidance and authoritarian decisions rarely solve the root problem.

stem: Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with type 1 diabetes who is newly confused, diaphoretic, and shaky.
options.why: New confusion with diaphoresis and tremors suggests acute hypoglycemia, which can rapidly cause seizures and brain injury; this acute, unexpected change is the priority.

options.text: A client with Alzheimer's disease who is oriented to person only, which is documented as the client's baseline.
options.why: Disorientation that matches a documented baseline is an expected chronic finding.

options.text: A client with chronic kidney disease whose potassium is 5.3 mEq/L and who is scheduled for dialysis this morning.
options.why: A mildly elevated potassium is expected in chronic kidney disease, and treatment (dialysis) is already planned.

options.text: A client with rheumatoid arthritis who reports 60 minutes of morning joint stiffness.
options.why: Morning stiffness is an expected finding of rheumatoid arthritis and is not life-threatening.

takeaway: Acute and unexpected beats chronic and expected, even when the chronic client's numbers look abnormal.

stem: A client with a new tracheostomy has four needs. Which should the nurse address first?

options.text: Anxiety about being unable to speak.
options.why: Psychosocial needs matter but come after physiological needs such as a patent airway.
Pain is a physiological need, but moderate pain is not as urgent as a threatened airway.

options.text: Worry about how the tracheostomy will look to others.
options.why: Body image is a self-esteem need, which is lower priority on Maslow's hierarchy.

options.text: Coarse, gurgling respirations with SpO2 decreasing from 96% to 90%.
options.why: Gurgling respirations and falling oxygen saturation indicate secretions blocking the airway; airway is the first priority, and the nurse should suction.

takeaway: Use Maslow and ABCs: airway problems come before pain, safety, and psychosocial needs.

stem: An RN from the surgical unit is floated to a medical-cardiac unit for the shift. Which client should the charge nurse assign to the float nurse?

options.text: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis receiving an insulin infusion that requires hourly titration.
options.why: A complex, titrated, high-alert infusion is better assigned to a nurse familiar with the unit's protocols.

options.text: A client with cellulitis of the leg receiving IV antibiotics every 8 hours.
options.why: A stable client with care needs similar to those on a surgical unit (IV antibiotics, wound and skin assessment) is the best match for a float nurse.

options.text: A client with new-onset atrial fibrillation receiving a diltiazem infusion titrated to heart rate.
options.why: Titrating a cardiac drip on telemetry requires specialty experience the float nurse may not have.

options.text: A client with unstable angina who has new chest pain and is scheduled for cardiac catheterization in 1 hour.
options.why: An unstable cardiac client should be cared for by an experienced unit nurse.

takeaway: Assign float staff stable clients whose care resembles their usual practice; keep unstable or specialty-protocol clients with unit staff.

stem: A UAP reports the following data. Which finding requires the RN's immediate follow-up?

options.text: A temperature of 37.6 °C (99.7 °F) in a client 1 day after surgery.
options.why: A low-grade temperature is common in the first 24-48 hours after surgery and is not an emergency.

options.text: Urine output of 240 mL over the past 8 hours.
options.why: 240 mL over 8 hours is 30 mL/hr, which meets the usual minimum for adequate urine output.

options.text: Blood pressure 86/50 mmHg and heart rate 122/min in a client whose earlier blood pressure was 128/76 mmHg.
options.why: Hypotension with tachycardia is an acute change suggesting bleeding or shock; the RN must assess the client immediately.
Reduced appetite should be noted but is not urgent.

takeaway: The RN must personally follow up on any UAP report that suggests instability, such as new hypotension with tachycardia.

stem: A hospital activates its disaster plan and asks nurses to identify clients who can be discharged to make room for incoming casualties. Which client is most appropriate to discharge?

options.text: A client 6 hours after an open bowel resection.
options.why: A client in the immediate postoperative period after major surgery needs ongoing monitoring for bleeding and complications.

options.text: A client with an upper gastrointestinal bleed whose hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL and who is awaiting a blood transfusion.
options.why: Active bleeding with significant anemia requiring transfusion makes this client unstable.

options.text: A client with a COPD exacerbation who intermittently requires BiPAP.
options.why: A client who still needs noninvasive ventilation has an ongoing breathing problem and is not ready for discharge.

options.text: A client with pneumonia who has been afebrile for 48 hours, has an SpO2 of 95% on room air, and now takes oral antibiotics.
options.why: This client is stable, improving, oxygenating on room air, and on oral therapy, so care can safely continue at home.

takeaway: In a disaster, discharge stable, improving clients whose remaining care can be given at home or as outpatients.

stem: Which activity must the RN perform and NOT assign to a licensed practical nurse (LPN)?

options.text: Performing the initial assessment of a newly admitted client.
options.why: Initial assessment and the nursing care plan are RN responsibilities; the LPN may collect data and contribute to ongoing assessment.

options.text: Administering a scheduled oral antihypertensive to a stable client.
options.why: Giving oral medications to stable clients is within LPN scope of practice.

options.text: Reinforcing discharge teaching that the RN has already provided.
options.why: LPNs may reinforce teaching; they may not provide the initial teaching.

options.text: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter in a stable client.
options.why: Sterile procedures such as urinary catheter insertion are within LPN scope.

takeaway: RN-only: initial assessment, care planning, initial teaching, evaluation, and care of unstable clients.

stem: After performing hand hygiene, which sequence should the nurse use to put on personal protective equipment (PPE) before entering a client's room?

options.why: Putting gloves on first prevents the glove cuffs from covering the gown cuffs and risks contaminating the gloves while putting on other items.
CDC donning order is gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, then gloves pulled over the gown cuffs.
Gloves must go on last so they cover the gown cuffs and stay clean.
Putting the gown on last means it is tied over the gloves and other equipment, which is incorrect.

takeaway: Donning: gown, mask/respirator, goggles/face shield, gloves (gloves last).

stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. The nurse is wearing a gown, gloves, a face shield, and a surgical mask. Which removal sequence is correct?

options.why: Removing the mask first while still wearing contaminated gloves risks contaminating the face and mucous membranes.
The gloves are the most contaminated item and should come off first (or together with the gown), and the mask should come off last.
Touching the face shield and mask with contaminated gloves risks exposure of the face.

options.text: Gloves, face shield, gown, mask, then hand hygiene
options.why: CDC doffing order removes the most contaminated items first: gloves, face shield or goggles, gown, then mask, followed by hand hygiene.

takeaway: Doffing: gloves, goggles/face shield, gown, mask/respirator, then hand hygiene (mask last; remove a respirator after leaving the room).

stem: After caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection, which hand hygiene method should the nurse use?

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rub, rubbing until the hands are dry.
options.why: Alcohol does not reliably kill C. diff spores.

options.text: Rinsing the hands under running water without soap.
options.why: Water alone does not remove spores and organisms effectively.

options.text: Washing with soap and water, using friction.
options.why: The mechanical friction and rinsing of soap-and-water handwashing physically remove C. diff spores, which alcohol does not kill.

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rub followed immediately by a new pair of gloves.
options.why: Gloves over hands that still carry spores do not solve the problem; soap and water are required.

takeaway: C. diff: contact precautions, soap-and-water handwashing, and bleach-based (sporicidal) cleaning.

stem: A client with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is in an airborne infection isolation room and must be transported to radiology. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Place a surgical mask on the client for transport.
options.why: A surgical mask on the client contains respiratory droplets at the source; clients may leave the room for essential tests when masked.

options.text: Place a fit-tested N95 respirator on the client for transport.
options.why: N95 respirators protect staff from inhaling droplet nuclei; for source control the client wears a surgical mask.

options.text: Postpone the test until the client has three negative sputum smears.
options.why: Necessary diagnostic tests should not be delayed; a masked client can be transported safely.

options.text: Have the transporter wear a surgical mask while the client remains unmasked.
options.why: A surgical mask does not protect the wearer from airborne droplet nuclei, and an unmasked client spreads organisms along the route.

takeaway: Airborne (TB): negative-pressure room, fit-tested N95 for staff, surgical mask on the client when outside the room.

stem: A client is admitted with fever, nuchal rigidity, and a petechial rash. Bacterial meningitis is suspected, and IV antibiotics have been started. Which precautions should the nurse implement?

options.text: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room.
options.why: Meningococcal disease spreads by large respiratory droplets, not airborne droplet nuclei, so a negative-pressure room is not required.

options.text: Droplet precautions in a private room until 24 hours after effective antibiotic therapy begins.
options.why: Neisseria meningitidis spreads by droplets; a private room and a surgical mask for staff are needed until 24 hours of effective therapy.
Contact precautions do not protect against respiratory droplets.

options.text: Standard precautions only, because antibiotics have already been started.
options.why: The client remains infectious until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy have been completed.

takeaway: Meningococcal meningitis: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

stem: An 80-year-old client at high risk for falls becomes confused at night. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.why: Four raised side rails count as a restraint, and confused clients who climb over them fall from a greater height.

options.text: Apply a vest restraint during the night.
options.why: Restraints are a last resort, require a prescription, and can increase injury and agitation.
Sedatives increase confusion and fall risk in older adults.

options.text: Keep the bed low and locked, the call light in reach, and round hourly.
options.why: These are least-restrictive, evidence-based fall prevention measures.

takeaway: Fall prevention: low, locked bed, call light in reach, scheduled rounding and toileting; avoid four side rails and sedatives.

stem: A client has bilateral soft wrist restraints to prevent removal of an endotracheal tube. Which finding reported by the UAP requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: The fingers of the right hand are pale and cool, with capillary refill of 4 seconds.
options.why: Pale, cool fingers with delayed capillary refill indicate impaired circulation; the nurse must assess and loosen or reapply the restraint right away.

options.text: The restraints are tied to the bed frame with quick-release knots.
options.why: Securing to the bed frame (not the side rail) with a quick-release knot is correct practice.

options.text: Two fingers fit between each restraint and the client's wrist.
options.why: A two-finger fit is the correct tightness.

options.text: Skin checks and range of motion were done on each wrist 1 hour ago.
options.why: Releasing each limb for skin checks, range of motion, and toileting at least every 2 hours is correct; this was done on time.

takeaway: Monitor restrained limbs for circulation, sensation, and skin; tie to the bed frame with a quick-release knot, never to the side rail.

stem: The nurse discovers smoke and flames in a client's room. What is the nurse's first action?

options.why: Alarm is the second step of RACE, after rescuing anyone in immediate danger.

options.text: Close the doors to the room and the corridor.
options.why: Containing the fire is the third step of RACE.

options.text: Remove the client from immediate danger.
options.why: RACE begins with Rescue: move clients in immediate danger away from the fire first.

options.text: Use a fire extinguisher on the flames.
options.why: Extinguishing (using PASS) is the last step and only if the fire is small and safe to fight.

takeaway: RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish; extinguisher use is PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.

stem: While the nurse is giving morning medications, the client says, "That white pill is not the one I usually take." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that generic medications often look different and give the pill.
options.why: This may be true, but giving the drug without checking ignores a possible medication error.

options.text: Withhold the pill and verify it against the prescription and with the pharmacy.
options.why: A client's concern about a medication should always be investigated before administration to make sure the right drug and dose are being given.

options.text: Give the other medications and document that the client refused the white pill.
options.why: The client raised a question rather than refusing, and the possible error still needs investigation.

options.text: Ask the client to take the pill now and tell the provider about the concern later.
options.why: Giving a medication that may be wrong and checking later puts the client at risk.

takeaway: When a client questions a medication, stop and verify before giving it.

stem: Before giving a medication, which action best verifies the client's identity?

options.text: Check the room and bed number against the medication administration record.
options.why: Room and bed numbers are never acceptable identifiers because clients move and can be in the wrong bed.

options.text: Call out the client's name and wait for a response.
options.why: A confused, drowsy, or hard-of-hearing client may answer to any name.

options.text: Rely on recognizing the client from earlier in the shift.
options.why: Recognition is not a verified identifier and can lead to errors with similar-looking clients.

options.text: Ask the client to state their name and date of birth, and compare them with the ID band.
options.why: Two client-specific identifiers stated by the client and matched to the band and record meet patient safety standards.

takeaway: Use two identifiers (such as name and date of birth), never the room number, and have the client state them.

stem: Fifteen minutes after a unit of packed red blood cells is started, the client reports chills and low back pain. Temperature has risen from 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) to 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), and blood pressure has dropped from 124/76 to 92/58 mmHg. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank.
options.why: Notification is required but comes after the transfusion is stopped to limit further exposure.

options.text: Obtain blood and urine samples for laboratory testing.
options.why: Samples are collected per protocol after the transfusion is stopped and the client is stabilized.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing.
options.why: These signs suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stopping the blood limits the amount of incompatible blood given, and new tubing keeps the IV access open without giving the blood left in the old tubing.

options.text: Slow the transfusion and give acetaminophen as prescribed.
options.why: Slowing the infusion continues to give incompatible blood, and acetaminophen does not treat a hemolytic reaction.

takeaway: For any suspected transfusion reaction, first stop the transfusion and keep the vein open with normal saline through new tubing.

stem: The nurse sets up a sterile field for a dressing change. Which event requires the nurse to discard the field and set up a new one?

options.text: The nurse left the room briefly to get a forgotten supply, leaving the field unattended.
options.why: A sterile field that is out of the nurse's sight is considered contaminated, because sterility cannot be confirmed.

options.text: The nurse dropped sterile gauze onto the center of the field from about 15 cm (6 inches) above it.
options.why: Dropping sterile items onto the field without touching it is the correct technique.

options.text: The nurse opened the first flap of the sterile package away from the body.
options.why: Opening the first flap away from the body is correct and avoids reaching over the field.

options.text: The nurse poured sterile saline into a sterile basin with the label facing the palm.
options.why: Pouring with the label against the palm protects the label and does not contaminate the field.

takeaway: A sterile field must stay in view; unattended, below waist level, wet-through, or touched by nonsterile items means contaminated.

stem: Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care to prevent pressure injury in an immobile client?

options.text: Massage reddened areas over bony prominences.
options.why: Massaging reddened skin can damage fragile tissue and is not recommended.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower and reposition at least every 2 hours.
options.why: A low head-of-bed angle reduces shear and sliding, and regular repositioning relieves pressure on bony prominences.

options.text: Use a ring (donut) cushion when the client sits in a chair.
options.why: Ring cushions concentrate pressure on surrounding tissue and reduce circulation.

options.text: Place several layers of linen and underpads under the client to absorb moisture.
options.why: Extra layers trap heat and moisture and reduce the effect of pressure-redistributing surfaces; use a single breathable pad and manage moisture directly.

takeaway: Prevent pressure injury with regular repositioning, head of bed 30 degrees or lower, pressure-redistributing surfaces, and no massage of red skin.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who will use oxygen at home. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will put 'No Smoking' signs in my home."
options.why: This is correct; smoking near oxygen is a major fire risk.

options.text: "I will keep my oxygen at least 10 feet away from the gas stove and candles."
options.why: This is correct; oxygen should be kept well away from open flames and heat sources.

options.text: "I will put petroleum jelly in my nose when it feels dry."
options.why: Petroleum-based products are flammable in an oxygen-rich environment; the client should use a water-based lubricant.

options.text: "I will store my extra oxygen tanks upright and secured."
options.why: This is correct; securing tanks prevents them from falling and being damaged.

takeaway: Home oxygen: no smoking or open flames nearby, water-based lubricants only, secure tanks upright.

stem: Which action by the nurse demonstrates correct body mechanics when moving a client or equipment?

options.text: Keeping a wide base of support and holding the load close to the body.
options.why: A wide base of support improves stability, and keeping the load close reduces strain on the back.

options.text: Bending at the waist with the knees straight to lift.
options.why: Bending at the waist strains the lower back; the nurse should bend at the hips and knees.

options.text: Twisting at the trunk to turn while carrying the load.
options.why: Twisting while lifting is a common cause of back injury; the nurse should pivot the feet instead.

options.text: Lifting a dependent adult client alone when no lift device is nearby.
options.why: Safe patient handling requires lift devices or additional staff for dependent clients.

takeaway: Body mechanics: wide base, load close, bend knees not waist, pivot don't twist, and use lift devices for dependent clients.

stem: A client receives NPH (intermediate-acting) insulin subcutaneously at 0700. During which time period is the client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia?

options.why: This matches the onset of rapid-acting insulin (about 15 minutes), not NPH.
NPH begins to act only 1 to 2 hours after injection, so peak risk is not this early.
NPH peaks about 4 to 12 hours after injection, so the greatest risk is from late morning through the afternoon; an afternoon snack helps prevent hypoglycemia.
NPH lasts about 12 to 18 hours, so its effect is mostly gone by the next morning.

takeaway: Know insulin peaks: rapid-acting 1-3 hours, regular 2-4 hours, NPH 4-12 hours; glargine has no pronounced peak.

stem: A client is receiving a continuous IV heparin infusion. The aPTT result is 118 seconds (therapeutic range per protocol: 60-85 seconds), and the client has pink-tinged urine. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion and notify the provider.
options.why: The aPTT is well above the therapeutic range and the client shows signs of bleeding; stopping the infusion is the priority, and the nurse should anticipate protamine sulfate if bleeding is significant.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; the heparin antidote is protamine sulfate.

options.text: Decrease the infusion rate by 2 mL/hr and recheck the aPTT in 6 hours.
options.why: A small rate reduction is not appropriate when the aPTT is markedly high and the client is actively bleeding.

options.text: Continue the infusion and send a urine sample for urinalysis.
options.why: Continuing heparin with active bleeding and a supratherapeutic aPTT puts the client at risk of serious hemorrhage.

takeaway: Heparin: monitor aPTT (or anti-Xa); for bleeding with a high value, stop the infusion, notify the provider, and anticipate protamine sulfate.

stem: A client with atrial fibrillation is being discharged on warfarin. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I can take ibuprofen for my arthritis pain."
options.why: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase the risk of bleeding with warfarin and should be avoided unless the provider approves.
The usual INR goal for atrial fibrillation is 2.0 to 3.0; an INR near 1.0 means no anticoagulant effect.

options.text: "If I bleed too much, protamine sulfate will reverse my warfarin."
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin; warfarin is reversed with vitamin K (phytonadione), and with prothrombin complex concentrate for serious bleeding.

options.text: "I will keep the amount of leafy green vegetables I eat about the same each week."
options.why: Vitamin K in leafy greens affects warfarin; a consistent intake, not avoidance, keeps the INR stable.

takeaway: Warfarin: INR goal usually 2-3, consistent vitamin K intake, avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless prescribed, antidote is vitamin K.

stem: Before giving digoxin 0.125 mg PO, the nurse finds an apical pulse of 64/min and a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. The client reports nausea and seeing yellow halos around lights. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose because the apical pulse is above 60/min.
options.why: A heart rate above 60 does not rule out toxicity; nausea and visual changes are classic signs of digoxin toxicity.

options.text: Withhold the dose and notify the provider.
options.why: Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity, and nausea with yellow visual halos suggests toxicity is already present; the nurse holds the dose and anticipates a digoxin level and potassium replacement.

options.text: Give the dose with a potassium-rich food such as a banana.
options.why: Food will not correct a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L quickly, and the toxicity signs mean the dose must be held.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the apical pulse in 1 hour.
options.why: Giving another dose to a client with signs of toxicity could cause dangerous dysrhythmias.

takeaway: Hold digoxin for signs of toxicity (nausea, vomiting, visual changes, dysrhythmias), even if the pulse is above 60; low potassium raises the risk.

stem: Which potassium chloride prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL, infused over 1 hour by infusion pump through a peripheral IV.
options.why: 10 mEq/hr is a commonly accepted maximum rate through a peripheral line when given by pump.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq added to 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride at 100 mL/hr.
options.why: This delivers 2 mEq/hr in a dilute solution, which is safe.

options.text: Potassium chloride 10 mEq IV push over 2 minutes.
options.why: IV potassium is never given by IV push; a rapid bolus can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO twice daily with meals.
options.why: Oral potassium with meals is appropriate and reduces gastrointestinal irritation.

takeaway: IV potassium: always diluted, on a pump, never IV push, and confirm adequate urine output first.

stem: Twenty minutes into an IV vancomycin infusion, the client develops flushing and an itchy red rash on the face, neck, and upper chest. Blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, and there is no wheezing or throat tightness. What should the nurse do first?

options.why: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis; this client has no hypotension, wheezing, or airway swelling.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate so the dose finishes sooner.
options.why: This reaction is caused by infusing too fast; speeding up makes it worse.

options.text: Continue the infusion and apply cool compresses to the rash.
options.why: Continuing at the same rate allows the reaction to progress.

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider.
options.why: These are signs of vancomycin infusion reaction (red man syndrome), a rate-related histamine release; stop the infusion, then expect to restart more slowly (over at least 60 minutes) with an antihistamine.

takeaway: Vancomycin: infuse over at least 60 minutes to prevent infusion reaction; monitor drug levels per protocol (AUC-guided dosing is now preferred; troughs are drawn just before the next dose), and monitor kidney function.

stem: A client receiving IV gentamicin reports ringing in the ears and dizziness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the provider.
options.why: Tinnitus and dizziness are signs of aminoglycoside ototoxicity, which can become permanent; the nurse holds the dose and anticipates drug levels and kidney function tests.

options.text: Explain that these are expected effects and continue the medication.
options.why: Ototoxicity is a serious adverse effect, not an expected one.

options.text: Give the dose and request a prescription for meclizine.
options.why: Treating the dizziness hides a sign of toxicity while the drug keeps causing damage.

options.text: Encourage extra fluids and give the next dose as scheduled.
options.why: Hydration supports the kidneys but does not reverse ototoxicity; giving more drug increases the harm.

takeaway: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin): watch for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; monitor levels, creatinine, and hearing.

stem: A client who had surgery today is using a morphine PCA pump. The client has a respiratory rate of 7/min, is difficult to arouse, and has an SpO2 of 86%. The nurse stops the PCA, stimulates the client, and supports ventilation. Which describes correct naloxone administration?

options.text: Give naloxone 2 mg rapid IV push to completely reverse the opioid.
options.why: Rapid full reversal can cause severe pain, withdrawal, hypertension, and dysrhythmias in a postoperative client.

options.text: Dilute naloxone 0.4 mg in 10 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and give small increments slowly, titrating to respiratory rate and level of consciousness.
options.why: Titrating diluted naloxone reverses respiratory depression while keeping as much pain relief as possible.

options.text: Give one dose, then stop monitoring once the respiratory rate is above 12/min because naloxone lasts longer than morphine.
options.why: Naloxone has a shorter duration than morphine, so respiratory depression can return; continued close monitoring is required.

options.text: Wait until the respiratory rate falls below 4/min before giving naloxone.
options.why: The client is already hypoxic and difficult to arouse; waiting risks respiratory arrest.

takeaway: Naloxone: titrate in small doses to breathing, not to full reversal, and keep monitoring because it wears off before most opioids.

stem: A client has a prescription for a heparin infusion at 1,200 units/hr. The pharmacy supplies heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL of D5W. At what rate should the nurse set the infusion pump?

options.why: This is a decimal error; it is ten times too low.
This is a decimal error; it is ten times too high and would cause a dangerous overdose.
25,000 units / 250 mL = 100 units/mL. 1,200 units/hr / 100 units/mL = 12 mL/hr.
This would be correct only for a concentration of 50 units/mL (for example, 25,000 units in 500 mL).

takeaway: Find the concentration first (units/mL), then divide the prescribed dose per hour by the concentration to get mL/hr.

stem: A child who weighs 22 lb has a prescription for acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO every 6 hours as needed for fever. The available liquid is 160 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.why: This divides 150 mg by 160 mg but forgets to multiply by the 5 mL volume.
22 lb / 2.2 = 10 kg. 10 kg x 15 mg/kg = 150 mg. 150 mg / 160 mg x 5 mL = 4.69 mL, rounded to 4.7 mL.
This inverts the ratio (160 / 150 x 5 mL) instead of dividing the desired dose by the dose on hand.
This uses the weight in pounds as kilograms (22 x 15 = 330 mg), more than doubling the dose.

takeaway: Convert pounds to kilograms first (divide by 2.2), then use desired dose / dose on hand x volume.

stem: A client with advanced lung cancer has a valid living will refusing intubation and mechanical ventilation, and a do-not-resuscitate prescription is in the chart. The client becomes unresponsive with severe respiratory distress. The client's adult son arrives and demands that the client be intubated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Prepare for intubation because the son is the next of kin.
options.why: A family member's wishes do not override a competent client's valid advance directive.

options.text: Ask the son to sign a form overriding the living will.
options.why: No such form exists; family members cannot cancel a client's legally valid advance directive.

options.text: Call the rapid response team to intubate while the ethics committee reviews the case.
options.why: Intubating would violate the client's documented wishes and the existing prescription.

options.text: Follow the advance directive, provide comfort measures, and ask the provider to meet with the son.
options.why: The nurse advocates for the client's documented wishes, keeps the client comfortable, and supports the family by arranging a discussion with the provider (and an ethics consult if conflict continues).

takeaway: A valid advance directive reflects the client's autonomy and is followed even when family members disagree.

stem: A caller says he is a client's brother and asks how the client is doing after surgery. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check whether the client has authorized release of information to this person.
options.why: Under HIPAA, health information is shared only with people the client has authorized (for example, through a listed contact or privacy code).

options.text: Give a brief update because family members are entitled to health information.
options.why: Being a relative does not by itself give a person the right to a client's health information.

options.text: Tell the caller the client's diagnosis but not the test results.
options.why: A diagnosis is protected health information and cannot be shared without authorization.

options.text: Ask the caller for the client's date of birth to prove the relationship, then give an update.
options.why: Knowing a date of birth does not prove the client has authorized disclosure to the caller.

takeaway: HIPAA: share health information only with people the client has authorized, and verify before you speak.

stem: A nurse tells a client, "I will be back in 15 minutes to help you walk," and returns on time even though the unit has become very busy. Which ethical principle is the nurse demonstrating?

options.why: Autonomy is respecting the client's right to make their own decisions.
Fidelity means keeping promises and being faithful to commitments made to the client.
Justice is fair and equal distribution of care and resources.
Veracity is telling the truth.

takeaway: Fidelity = keeping promises; veracity = truthfulness; autonomy = self-determination; justice = fairness; beneficence = doing good; nonmaleficence = doing no harm.

stem: Which situation best illustrates nursing malpractice?

options.text: A visitor slips on a wet hallway floor and sprains an ankle.
options.why: This may be ordinary negligence by the facility, but it does not involve a professional duty owed by a nurse to a client.

options.text: A nurse gives a scheduled medication 45 minutes late, and the client has no adverse effects.
options.why: Even if this is a breach of the standard of care, there is no harm, so the elements of malpractice are not met.

options.text: A nurse documents an assessment 2 hours after completing it, with no effect on the client's care.
options.why: Late documentation without harm does not meet the elements of malpractice.

options.text: An RN skips prescribed hourly dressing checks for 8 hours, and the client hemorrhages and needs a transfusion.
options.why: This meets all four elements of malpractice: a professional duty, breach of the standard of care, causation, and actual harm to the client.

takeaway: Malpractice is professional negligence and requires duty, breach, causation, and damages; negligence can be committed by anyone.

stem: At the start of a shift, a nurse notices that a coworker has slurred speech, an unsteady gait, and smells of alcohol. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Talk with the coworker privately after the shift.
options.why: Waiting until after the shift leaves clients in the care of an impaired nurse.

options.text: Report the observations immediately to the charge nurse or nursing supervisor.
options.why: Client safety comes first; reporting through the chain of command immediately gets the coworker removed from client care, and the facility follows its policy for further reporting and referral.

options.text: Report the coworker directly to the state board of nursing before telling anyone at the facility.
options.why: Board reporting may be required later, but it does not remove the coworker from client care right now.

options.text: Offer to take the coworker's highest-risk clients and watch for errors.
options.why: This enables the impaired coworker and still exposes clients to unsafe care.

takeaway: Suspected impairment on duty is reported immediately to the supervisor so the nurse is removed from client care.
